_doc: Single source for SD-29's technology choices (compact cut). Read by video/src/stack.py for the 5.1 technology slides, the stack table, the fix-slide 'Rejected' lines and the C4 technology labels, and by `stack.py sync` for the booklet and OUTLINE.md regions.

stack.heading: Device gateway: an MQTT broker cluster with mutual TLS
stack.title: MQTT over mutual TLS: one session per device, a certificate per device
stack.why: A small, battery-friendly protocol with persistent sessions and a device identity checked at the handshake.
stack.how: About 100,000 connections per node, 20 nodes. Each device presents its factory certificate; topics are scoped to its own ID.
stack.detail: MQTT 5 session expiry keeps a device's subscriptions for 7 days across disconnects. The broker forwards reported state and telemetry to Kafka through a bridge, and admits new connections through a per-node token bucket during storms. The desired-state document is served from a cache keyed by version, so a reconnecting device that is already current costs one comparison.
rejected: Every device polls whether or not anything changed.
A server-side log, not a device protocol.
summary: light sessions; identity at the handshake
stack.course: building-blocks course, part 11 §11.6–11.7 (persistent connections) and part 16 §16.1 (authentication)

stack.heading: Shadow store: desired and reported documents in PostgreSQL
stack.title: Two documents per device, each with a version
stack.why: 1 M rows of a few kilobytes is small; conditional updates on a version make every desired-state change a compare-and-set.
stack.how: One row per device: desired and reported JSON with versions. Writers use `WHERE desired_v = $read`.
stack.detail: About 4 GB in total. The reconciler reads the rows where `desired_v > reported_v` through an index on that difference. History of desired documents is kept in an append-only table for audit and for rollbacks: rolling back is writing an older document as a new version.
rejected: A lost write is a device told something nobody can see.
Six weeks offline means four obsolete configs.
stack.course: building-blocks course, part 15 §15.2 (desired state and reconciliation) and part 8 §8.2 (conditional writes)

stack.heading: Firmware images: signed, on object storage behind a CDN
stack.title: Signed images, fetched by range, verified on the device
stack.pick: Object storage + CDN; images signed offline
stack.why: 50 TB per release must not cross the gateway; a device-side signature check defeats a compromised CDN.
stack.how: The desired document names the URL, size, SHA-256 and an offline signature. The agent fetches by range, resumes, and verifies before writing.
stack.detail: Signing keys live in an HSM and sign release manifests in an offline ceremony; devices hold the public key from manufacture. Delta images reduce a typical release from 50 MB to about 8 MB.
rejected: 50 TB crowds out every control message.
TLS proves the server, not the image.
summary: the device verifies what it runs
stack.course: building-blocks course, part 7 §7.12 (integrity) and part 16 §16.4 (progressive rollout)

stack.heading: Telemetry: Kafka into a time-series store, by cohort
stack.title: Health aggregated by cohort, never labelled by device
stack.why: Rollout decisions compare cohorts and waves; a device-ID label would make a million series out of one metric.
stack.how: Summaries every 5 minutes with a per-device sequence; repeats dropped; metrics labelled by cohort, firmware and wave.
stack.detail: 3,300 messages a second, about 3.3 MB/s: small. Dedup state is the last sequence per device, 1 M entries. A device offline for weeks uploads its buffer oldest first at a capped rate.
stack.course: building-blocks course, part 14 §14.3 (cardinality) and part 10 §10.5 (delivery semantics)

1: a device that crashes on boot never connects to receive it.
2: 1 % is mostly the most common hardware; the rare revision that bricks may not be in it.
3: Replaying every queued change in order
a device offline for six weeks applies four obsolete configs to reach the fifth.
4: Immediate reconnect with a fixed retry
200,000 devices retry in step and the brokers never recover.
5: MQTT QoS 2 covers one session; a device replaying its buffer after a reboot is a new session.
6: a device that connects but runs the wrong firmware looks exactly healthy.
